title: The first milestone: two networked players
summary: The project began with a C++ server and two Godot clients, proving prediction, correction and remote movement before adding a world.
verificationStatus: Historical prototype verified
paragraphs: The first playable experiment was deliberately small: a standalone C++ server, two Godot clients and a diagnostic view of their positions. Clients sent movement intent, the server decided the result, and each client predicted its own motion while smoothing the other player. Getting that relationship working first gave later interface and world work a real multiplayer foundation.

Both ordinary local sessions and a bounded delay, jitter and packet-loss test completed without disconnects. A separate test deliberately displaced one client's prediction and confirmed that it returned to the server's position. Launchers also learned to clean up only the processes they owned, and the project gained its first Git checkpoint and asset versioning setup.

This was a two-player movement experiment on an empty plane. It did not include collision, weapons, inventory, persistence or a claim about internet-scale capacity. The custom transport was later replaced during the Unreal migration; the lesson that gameplay starts with authority remained.
highlights: Two actual clients observed each other
Intent, prediction, acknowledgement and correction connected
Deliberate prediction error recovered
Versioned project and repeatable launch workflow
limitations: Historical Godot/C++ transport, superseded by native Unreal networking
Two clients and collision-free motion only

title: An inventory that the server actually owns
summary: Inventory, equipment, crafting and shared-container interactions arrived as connected rules and interface behavior.
verificationStatus: Historical fixture tests passed
paragraphs: The next slice turned the network experiment into something that could be used: menus, a hotbar, inventory, equipment, a character preview, crafting and shared-container screens. Item movement was a request to the server, not a local subtraction followed by a hopeful update. Two players could observe changes to the same container while keeping their private inventories separate.

The recorded fixture tests exercised stack splitting, equipment appearance, timed crafting, ingredient deductions and cancellation refunds. They also checked that an outdated view could not duplicate loot or silently take a replacement item, and that changing container permission closed access. Those small consistency rules are the foundation of a future full-loot game.

These demonstrations used a temporary item and recipe catalog. That catalog was retired on 1 October so the project could concentrate on one real weapon slice. The rule layer and interaction design carried forward into the Unreal prototype, but this article is not a claim that the current test map contains crafting stations or loot-filled buildings.
highlights: Private inventory and public equipment separated
Shared loot changed for both players
Craft cancellation returned ingredients
Stale actions did not duplicate items
limitations: Temporary catalog and fixtures are historical
No death, corpse or persistent economy loop

title: Making the small interactions feel deliberate
summary: A series of interface passes refined splitting, quick looting, menu closure, typography and movement while the inventory is open.
verificationStatus: Historical controls tests passed
paragraphs: A working inventory still has to feel predictable. The interface gained whole-stack dragging, half and third splits, an amount slider and timed hover looting with independent progress indicators. Dropping outside a valid slot cancels the gesture. Starting several hover transfers does not force each circle to wait for the previous one.

Closing loot became immediate on screen, even while the server acknowledgement was still in flight. An older snapshot could no longer reopen the panel. Movement remained available through inventory and crafting screens, while typing into search correctly suppressed movement keys. Free-look, camera input, slot sizes, panel transparency and typography were refined in the same pass.

The important boundary stayed intact: the interface can respond immediately to a gesture, but the item total changes only after the authoritative result. Future wounded and respawn screens were recorded as design references, not added as imaginary completed systems.
highlights: Half, third and slider-based stack splits
Parallel hover-loot feedback
Immediate closing without stale-screen reopening
Movement and text entry use different input rules
limitations: Historical Godot interface validation
Wounded, death and respawn remained future work

title: Building a traceable world-art library
summary: World research became a bounded asset plan with preserved sources, acquisition records and isolated import checks.
verificationStatus: Historical acquisition and import checks
paragraphs: World production started with a practical question: which trees, terrain surfaces, cliffs and ground cover could actually be brought into the engine? The early art direction explored temperate, snow and desert regions, then narrowed the asset list to usable source formats. A single birch preview established scale, cutout transparency and lighting before the scene became a forest.

Fourteen supplied source files were checked against recorded sizes and hashes. Additional vegetation sources and the supplied resource-node models were inventoried and preserved. A supplied monument reference was retained for the prototype study. These were acquisition and adaptation tasks, not claims that the team modeled every rock, tree or building from scratch.

That distinction matters for the public journal too. The world work is about selection, conversion, materials and composition. Third-party originals remain credited, and keeping a source in the private working library does not make it a public download.
highlights: Three-biome art direction
Isolated birch import before mass placement
Source and acquisition records preserved
Resource-node inputs verified
limitations: Asset ownership and attribution vary by source
No public source-asset redistribution implied

title: The first world: forest, snow and desert
summary: A 1.5 km art study brought the terrain, vegetation, river, road and coastline together through eight visual passes.
verificationStatus: Historical art baseline accepted
paragraphs: The first world study covered roughly 1.5 km, with a saved heightfield, branching ridges, lowlands, a ravine, sandstone canyon, coastal inlets and a river reaching the sea. Its final land mix was approximately 40% temperate, 31% snow and 29% desert. Snow was a geographic region rather than a rule that simply painted every high point white.

Eight capture passes changed the scene substantially. A repeated northern mountain wall was rejected; overly smooth landforms, floating rocks, excessive fog, patterned road markings and water artifacts were corrected. Trees, undergrowth, wind, resource heaps, a road and a bridge gave the inspection scene enough variety to walk through and judge.

The result was accepted as a starting point and preserved. Its dense views still ran well below the eventual frame-rate target, and terrain following was an inspection aid rather than authoritative collision. This large art study is historical: today's character and weapon work uses a small flat test map.
highlights: Three geographic biomes across mixed terrain
Eight visual iteration passes
River, coastline, road and bridge composition
Preserved starting point with ground walkthrough
limitations: Art scene, not a production multiplayer map
Historical 36–110 FPS camera samples at 1600×900 on RTX 2070 SUPER
Water was visual and full terrain collision was absent

title: Keeping the world, reducing its cost
summary: The first optimization pass retained the scene's placements while improving foliage detail selection, culling and batching.
verificationStatus: Historical measured improvement; target missed
paragraphs: The next day started with the most expensive forest and river views. The optimization brief was to retain the world rather than solve performance by removing it. Work focused on when foliage changes detail, how canopy groups are culled and how repeated pieces are submitted for drawing.

All 449,063 visual placements were retained. Grouping monument meshes removed 214 separate drawables, and foliage detail-selection changes improved the matched heavy views. The final short camera samples ranged from about 48 to 139 FPS on the recorded machine and settings. That was progress, but it did not meet the newly clarified 144 FPS target across the world.

The evidence pointed toward rendering work rather than a blanket conclusion about an engine limit. The project preserved the measured result and opened an Unreal migration assessment instead of declaring the target reached.
highlights: Scene density and placements retained
Foliage detail and culling adjusted
Repeated meshes batched
144 FPS gap documented honestly
limitations: Short fixed-camera samples, not a traversal or multiplayer load test
Godot result superseded by the Unreal direction

title: Moving the prototype to Unreal
summary: The project moved to Unreal while keeping the rule layer and replacing the custom transport with native replication and RPCs.
verificationStatus: Historical build and native network checks passed
paragraphs: The engine migration preserved the useful engine-independent rules and rebuilt their runtime around Unreal's native networking. Listen hosting, private replicated inventory, public player appearance and reliable gameplay requests took over from the earlier custom transport. The interface was rebuilt with Slate, including its live character preview.

The world export was substantial: 526 unique meshes, 456,753 mesh instances, 144 terrain tiles and 478 texture references. Conversion had to preserve handedness, winding, scale, materials and actual instance transforms. An early exporter returned identity transforms for some instanced meshes; comparing the export with the running source scene caught the problem before it became an accepted map.

A real editor build succeeded, and two native processes passed five host and fifteen client checks. This was a working migration checkpoint, not a claim that every visual, interaction and performance acceptance gate had been completed.
highlights: Native Unreal replication replaced custom transport
Reusable C++ rules retained
World source transforms checked
Two-process host and client tests passed
limitations: Historical Unreal 5.8.2 checkpoint
Full visual and interaction parity remained incomplete

title: A package, real input and the limits of parity
summary: The native build became a standalone package, while interaction testing separated widget behavior from real operating-system input.
verificationStatus: Historical package and scoped interaction checks
paragraphs: The migrated prototype produced a standalone development package and passed the same small host/client network exercise. Nine direct widget-handler checks covered splitting, slider dragging, outside-drop cancellation, closing stale loot and parallel hover transfers. Portrait lighting, font scale, colors and icon sizing also received targeted corrections.

Real input testing added a different kind of evidence. Holding movement through inventory and crafting transitions worked, search focus suppressed movement, and Tab closed the interface from the search field. Later gesture phases did not complete, so those three observations stayed separate from a full input-suite pass.

Connection-failure handling was improved too: an occupied requested port should report failure rather than silently select another one. The newest source fix was initially newer than the package, and the records explicitly kept that distinction. A runnable package is useful; it is not automatically the latest validated build.
highlights: Standalone development build produced
Nine widget interaction checks passed
Three real-input behaviors observed
Clearer session failure reporting
limitations: Remaining focus and gesture checks were incomplete
Historical package does not contain later controller work
No packaged dedicated-server qualification

title: Faster in Unreal did not mean finished
summary: The world rendered faster in the recorded Unreal tests, but dense forest still missed the target and two instancing experiments were rejected.
verificationStatus: Historical measured results; rejected candidates retained
paragraphs: Unreal brought a significant improvement in the sampled world views, but the forest and river remained the hard cases. The final packaged forest sample averaged about 105 FPS at 1600×900 on an RTX 2070 SUPER. That is a recorded view on a specific machine, not a promise about the whole game or a 144 FPS minimum.

Profiling identified substantial shadow, base-pass and render-visibility work. Switching the whole scene to a GPU-driven instancing candidate made the forest slower, and a spatially divided version also lost to the reference. Both candidates were rejected. Keeping the faster reference mattered more than adopting a technique because its name sounded newer.

Material correctness continued alongside performance: source normal reconstruction, vegetation masks and startup sky lighting were repaired. The work ended at a preserved checkpoint with the frame-rate gap still open. The current flat controller map must not be used to imply that the old forest problem has been solved.
highlights: Actual packaged forest measurement recorded
Rendering costs profiled
Two slower instancing candidates rejected
Material and lighting correctness retained
limitations: 144 FPS target remained unmet
No player-capacity or server-load result
No completed forward-renderer comparison

title: Making the editor a repeatable workbench
summary: VibeUE integration, explicit project launching and preserved evidence made editor work easier to repeat and inspect.
verificationStatus: Tooling installed and connection verified
paragraphs: Development resumed with the editor workflow itself. VibeUE was installed and verified, giving the project a consistent route for scripted Unreal inspection, repeatable play sessions and real game captures. Project configuration enabled the editor connection automatically after a restart.

A recurring recent-project launch problem was traced to project discovery, and explicit project launching recovered the valid build. The workflow now checks the loaded map and build identity before making changes. This is unglamorous work, but it prevents a good test from being attributed to the wrong binary or a world edit from landing in the wrong level.

The same discipline shaped later work: preserve failed runs, record what a check actually covers, and look at the captured game view instead of trusting its filename. Tools are useful when they make the result more inspectable.

Project connection starts automatically
Reliable explicit project launching
Build and visual evidence kept together

title: Writing down what the server must become
summary: The architecture review separated the working prototype from the requirements for responsive, persistent full-loot PvP.
verificationStatus: Documented design; future gates remain open
paragraphs: The server review established a clear direction: one authoritative Unreal world, responsive local controls, private inventory views and deliberate ownership rules. It also separated things that had actually worked in two-player tests from things the game would need before public persistent play.

The development order became explicit: qualify the controller and dedicated-server path, build one complete disposable combat loop, then add identity and persistence before making measured capacity or production claims. Combat responsiveness remains central; the design avoids making every shot wait for a disk write while still requiring coherent economic recovery later.

This was architecture work, not a new backend deployment. Authentication, storage, large-world replication, recovery and player capacity remained future gates. The plan also left broad world features open instead of treating every feature from a reference game as a commitment.
highlights: Implemented behavior separated from requirements
Responsive PvP made explicit
Staged development gates recorded
No unmeasured population promise
limitations: Documentation, not implementation of persistence or production hosting
Historical test receipts were not automatically rerun

title: A physical controller and a steady view
summary: Native movement brought walking, sprinting, crouching and jumping together with a camera independent of animation.
verificationStatus: Scoped controller and camera tests passed
paragraphs: The new controller used Unreal's physical character movement for walking, falling, jumping and crouching. Sprint intent traveled through the movement prediction path. A stable camera followed the capsule and player input, while animated head motion stayed cosmetic. The chosen feel keeps locomotion headbob off and allows independent Alt free-look.

The first two-client checks found a surprisingly large problem: the sky mesh had blocking collision and was pushing the physical player out of the test area. Correcting that collision and adding a second spawn made grounded movement testable. A corrected controller run passed 27 assertions, and a later camera-focused run passed 38 while showing that animated head movement did not move the view.

These were two clients and a dedicated server inside one editor process. The early character geometry was temporary, and its owner look-down framing still needed work. Physical movement and a stable view were real progress, but neither result completed the independent-client or packaged-server gate.
highlights: Native walk, sprint, jump and crouch
Camera independent of animated bones
Sky collision corrected
27 controller and 38 camera checks in separate runs
limitations: Separate historical scenarios on their recorded builds
Single-process dedicated editor testing
Initial character presentation was temporary

title: Studying bodies, viewmodels and weapon motion
summary: Local character and service-pistol research examined separate rigs, source transforms and the gap between preserved animation data and a runtime match.
verificationStatus: Local study and numerical audits; limited visual scope
paragraphs: A local Rust reference study examined how the full body, head and dedicated first-person arms differ. The useful result was a clearer separation between world presentation and the player's viewmodel. A clothed arm rig could not simply be treated as the bare character, and unused leg bones did not prove that a viewmodel actually contained leg geometry.

The study preserved mesh binding and source transforms through export, prepared readable Blender previews and recovered a small unarmed set plus a larger indexed first-person animation library. A numerical audit checked timing and rotation structure across the accepted library. Playback tools were corrected so changing an action also changed the preview range; otherwise a long reload could appear to loop only its first frames.

The supplied service-pistol model was fitted to a local M92 animation study. The work needed more than a static grip: the reference weapon has independently animated parts and its own hierarchy. Retaining only a generic prop attachment would lose part of that motion.

The study recovered the weapon hierarchy, calibrated replacement parts against the assembled idle and preserved defaults for parts that a particular clip does not animate. Attack selection and the difference between ordinary idle and aimed idle were checked. The viewer also received reliable clip ranges so the full reload could be inspected.

These are third-party Rust assets used for private research and prototype work. They are not original project art, not a public asset release, and not proof of exact native playback. Structural checks and a few inspected clips cannot certify an entire animation library.

This was a compatibility and presentation study using third-party animation references. It did not add a firing controller, ammunition, damage or reload rules to the game. The later runtime import deliberately admitted only the idle that passed its fit checks.

Source bind transforms preserved
16-clip unarmed study and indexed FPS library
Independent weapon-part motion retained
Pistol replacement fit calibrated
Playback ranges corrected for action switching

No native Unity comparison for all recovered clips
Numerical library audit is not complete visual acceptance
Offline pistol study did not implement firing, reload or damage

title: Replacing the placeholder character
summary: The local prototype moved to the selected reference character, with separate first-person arms, synchronized body presentation and repaired materials.
verificationStatus: Historical numeric pass; visual acceptance later withdrawn
paragraphs: The temporary Survival Character presentation first received shared owner geometry, synchronized movement and wearable visibility rules. It also exposed a real input issue: mouse sensitivity was being scaled twice. Removing the inherited multiplier restored the intended setting, and the new checks exercised the actual input path rather than calling the look function directly.

The chosen Rust reference body and head then replaced that placeholder in the private prototype, with a separate first-person arm rig and original idle study. Material setup and wrist handling were corrected, and confirmed inventory state controlled whether the arms and held item appeared. A 76-assertion run verified its sampled camera, rig and equipment invariants.

The visual result was subsequently rejected. Crouch and locomotion still produced unacceptable anatomy, and body turning was incomplete. The numeric pass remains useful evidence of its narrow checks, but it does not turn that rejected presentation into a success. The third-party geometry remains reference material, not an original-art claim.

Owner and observer presentation synchronized
Separate first-person rig integrated
Material and wrist checks added

title: Two hundred checks can still miss the point
summary: The anatomy pass improved measured invariants and equipment behavior, but the movement was still rejected in visual review.
verificationStatus: Numeric checks passed; visual result rejected
paragraphs: The next correction tackled crouch space, leg lanes, limb lengths, stance and cosmetic head/body turning. It also made the starting state unequipped: selecting a belt slot raised its item, and selecting it again lowered it. Free-look was separated from ordinary aim, including a correction for an offset being applied twice.

The resulting run passed 200 sampled assertions across movement, camera, look and equipment states. Those tests had value, but visual review still rejected the result. Procedural gait and owner torso adjustments could satisfy numeric bounds while producing an unconvincing body in motion.

That rejection changed the next step. More assertions were not a substitute for better motion and direct visual review. The failed appearance and its passing numerical record were both preserved, and the project moved toward authored locomotion and a cleaner first-person lower-body solution.

Default unequipped state and same-slot toggle
Free-look double counting corrected
Rejected visual result kept in the record
limitations: 200/200 was a scoped numerical result, not visual acceptance

title: A body-animation recovery that did not make the cut
summary: A 44-clip offline reconstruction preserved data but failed the appearance test and was excluded from gameplay.
verificationStatus: Rejected offline experiment
paragraphs: A separate experiment tried to reconstruct full-body reference animation from Humanoid data without native engine evaluation. It produced an offline 44-clip library covering locomotion, crouching, swimming, jumping and turning, with synchronized body and head action slots in the viewer.

Package and playback checks confirmed that the exported data was present and repeatable. They did not recreate the original engine's complete animation behavior. Missing runtime solving, layering and other evaluation details mattered: the preview was reported as broken, including head/body separation, and its earlier usability claim was withdrawn.

The result was kept as research and explicitly excluded from gameplay. A failed experiment can still identify the next real test, but its file count is not a feature count. The later locomotion replacement used a different, authored retargeting route.

title: Replacing generated gait with authored motion
summary: Eighteen authored clips replaced procedural leg movement, with shared stride timing, smoother reversals and a better jump transition.
verificationStatus: Scoped authored-motion checks passed
paragraphs: The rejected generated gait was replaced with 18 Epic-authored sequences retargeted to the private prototype's existing reference skeleton. The set covers idle, directional walking, running, crouching and airborne states. The first-person body and observer body share the same motion snapshot and gait clock instead of advancing independently.

The runtime follows all 33 recorded stride cycles across the moving clips, blends direction changes continuously and eases the jump apex into falling. A one-time crouch-height correction preserved the measured foot positions across 202 keyed frames rather than adding a runtime leg solver. The camera remains independent throughout.

The first full-motion run passed 106 assertions on its recorded build. Later tests and the final owner-body run have their own identities. None of these results claims original Rust locomotion parity or perfect foot contact in every rendered condition; continuous motion review remains its own job.

title: Looking down without folding the character
summary: A dedicated lower-body derivative replaced rejected torso-folding experiments while preserving the shared authored leg pose.
verificationStatus: Bounded still review and 79-assertion motion pass
paragraphs: First-person look-down framing had become the stubborn problem. Folding the upper torso or moving the pelvis inside the pose produced an intrusive abdomen or warped silhouette. Those candidates were rejected, including attempts that looked numerically safe.

The accepted bounded solution uses the reference character's original legs and feet with a small weighted waist closure. The whole cosmetic component moves together for framing, while the authored pose, observer body, camera and collision remain independent. Four real game stills covered standing, crouched, crouch-walking and running views.

A corrected full-motion scenario then completed all 79 assertions. Earlier failures remain failures: one lacked transition coverage, and another expected intermediate observer velocity values that the engine does not promise. Correcting the test and executing the full suite supplied new evidence; it did not retroactively pass the old runs. Wrong-viewport image exports were also rejected instead of being presented as motion footage.

title: A sprint correction should remember the original move
summary: Forward-only sprint now retains the move's original direction decision when prediction is replayed after a correction.
verificationStatus: Bounded direction and correction tests passed
paragraphs: Sprint was narrowed to meaningful forward input rather than diagonal, lateral or backward travel. That exposed a subtle correction problem: when the client replays an old saved move, the character may already be facing a new direction. Rechecking the old acceleration against today's facing can incorrectly reinterpret a forward sprint as a strafe.

The movement path now preserves the original move's direction decision for replay. Ordinary prediction and the server still use the normal eligibility rule. The correction test forced an actual position discrepancy under configured client delay, observed the replay path and confirmed recovery. A separate 17-case direction suite passed too.

These checks add useful confidence to a specific movement edge case. They are not a broad adverse-network certification, and the configured delay should not be advertised as a measured round-trip time.

Saved move retains its direction decision
Actual correction replay exercised
Separate directional cases verified

title: Removing the stop-start chatter from turning
summary: Stationary body rotation now follows a continuous mouse sweep and settles when the input actually becomes quiet.
verificationStatus: Six-sweep owner and observer checks passed
paragraphs: The first stationary-turn rule had an obvious rhythm: wait, catch up, stop, then repeat during the same continuous look. The revised behavior keeps a turn active across continuing input and gaps between observer updates. Angular speed eases instead of snapping between active and idle.

Fast sweeps also need enough follow speed to avoid falling so far behind that the shortest rotation reverses at the angle wrap. The new response adapts to that input while preserving the small initial look allowance. The player camera and physical capsule do not inherit the cosmetic turning motion.

Six sweeps covering both directions, reversal, fast turning and crouch produced 1,434 sampled frames and passed 15 assertions. Each sweep had one start and one settle in the tested conditions. Continuous visual review and wider observer-network conditions remain separate from this scoped result.
highlights: Continuous turning through sustained look
Smoother angular-speed response
Fast-wrap reversal avoided
Owner and observer sampled together
limitations: Single-process dedicated editor test
No complete impaired-network animation qualification

title: One pistol, a cleaner starting point
summary: The active placeholder catalog was retired in favor of a single service pistol with verified idle presentation and a calibrated observer grip.
verificationStatus: Idle presentation verified; full clip export rejected
paragraphs: The active content baseline was reduced to one service pistol. Old placeholder identities were retired instead of recycled, and development sessions began with the pistol stored but unequipped. This keeps the next gameplay work focused on one complete weapon path rather than a large catalog of unfinished stand-ins.

The first-person presentation combines the reference arms and weapon hierarchy into a single skinned mesh playing the validated idle animation. The world grip needed anatomical calibration because the first-person and body rigs use different wrist and finger bases. Copying rotations directly had inverted the grip; the corrected mapping preserved bone lengths and aligned the observer weapon without a duplicate owner gun.

A fresh editor build passed 24 pistol assertions; separate standalone tests passed 86 catalog and rule checks, with a bounded review of real first-person and observer stills. The full animation export still failed a reload-part fit check and was excluded. At this verified checkpoint, holding the pistol is implemented; firing, reload logic, recoil and damage are not a completed combat feature.

Stable retired item identities
Combined first-person idle and calibrated world grip
Failed full-animation candidate excluded

title: Keeping command work bounded and inventory private
summary: The multiplayer foundation now rejects excess work predictably and updates affected private views instead of rebuilding everyone's state for an ordinary action.
verificationStatus: Build, deterministic checks and scoped multiplayer pass
paragraphs: Before extending combat, the command path received a focused foundation pass. Incoming gameplay work is bounded, invalid requests preserve state, and rejected ordinary commands can recover through the normal queue. Requests also need a valid gameplay owner. These are practical prototype safeguards, not a claim of production security.

Private inventory publication became more selective. An action marks the affected owner, changes are grouped before publication, and unchanged views retain their revision. Cached object projections reduce repeated work. The goal is straightforward: one player's private action should not cause unrelated inventories to rebuild or receive artificial changes.

The checkpoint retained 1,310 deterministic checks and passed a corrected 35-assertion dedicated editor scenario after two earlier test-harness failures. The correction made the probe deliver real client requests before judging the result. Conservation, ordinary-command recovery and owner isolation passed; shared-container integration, independent clients, broader network conditions and capacity remain open.

Inventory conservation through rejected actions
Affected-owner publication
1,310 deterministic checks and 35 runtime assertions

title: Designing the next reusable weapon foundation
summary: The project checkpoint now separates completed presentation from the shared item-instance and combat behavior being designed next.
verificationStatus: Design direction; implementation work not claimed complete
paragraphs: The repository was cleaned into an Unreal-focused baseline while preserving useful source assets and historical evidence. The project summary was rewritten around what can actually be played: networked movement, inventory/equip and pistol holding presentation. Old world, catalog and packaging successes remain in the history with their original limits.

The next weapon should be reusable. Shared definitions describe a weapon, while an individual item retains its own state when moved or equipped. That avoids a magazine that belongs to a slot or magically resets when the player raises the gun. The intended player-facing combat direction includes meaningful travel, hit locations and a deliberate policy for latency, with exact behavior still requiring design and validation.

This is the direction beyond the last verified checkpoint, not a finished combat announcement. The complete death, loot and respawn loop, persistent accounts, production hosting and measured capacity remain later milestones. The journal will record those as completed only when their own evidence exists.

Historical source and failed evidence preserved
Shared definitions separated from individual weapon state
Next gameplay milestone stated explicitly
limitations: Design review is not a build or gameplay pass
This entry describes design direction; completed weapon gameplay is not claimed
No release date or capacity promise

title: The pistol becomes a combat prototype
summary: The reusable weapon foundation now connects individual magazines, reserve ammunition, reloading and aiming to server-resolved bullet flight and damage.
verificationStatus: Implemented and built; qualification incomplete
paragraphs: The service pistol has moved beyond holding presentation. A shared weapon definition now supplies its behavior, while each individual weapon keeps its loaded ammunition and firing state when moved through the inventory. Raising the gun does not refill it. Reloading transfers compatible reserve ammunition when the action completes, and interruption preserves the rounds already loaded.

Firing has its own network path so it does not wait behind ordinary inventory actions. The player gets immediate local feedback, then reconciles with the server's result. The server decides whether the action is valid, spends ammunition and advances a finite-speed bullet under gravity. Head, torso and limb queries determine damage, with current cover taking priority. A hit marker requires confirmed damage rather than the local firing effect alone.

Aiming, a procedural shot kick, flash, development audio and a reload-lowering cue surround the validated idle. The earlier rejected animation export remains excluded. These effects let the prototype communicate its actions while authored firing and reload presentation still need their own validation.

The successful editor build and recorded tests establish implemented prototype behavior, but the weapon milestone is not complete. The main regression suite still has unexecuted checks, and firing and reload need normal-speed visual review. Zero health currently stops further actions; it does not create the death, corpse, loot and respawn loop.

The recoil direction has also been clarified: each weapon should have a fixed, repeatable pattern that players can learn. In the build covered here, upward and alternating sideways impulses provided temporary feedback. Authored patterns and their runtime validation were the next step, separate from the existing accuracy spread.
highlights: Ammunition belongs to individual weapon instances
Reloads use actual inventory reserve ammunition
Firing is independent of the inventory queue
Server-resolved bullet travel, gravity and anatomical damage
Immediate feedback reconciles with authoritative results
limitations: Weapon core and temporal visual qualification remain incomplete
Fixed learnable recoil patterns were still a requirement at this build checkpoint
Only the validated idle animation is integrated
No completed death, loot, respawn or persistent combat loop

title: Testing the shot while everything keeps moving
summary: Delay, moving targets and a distant cover test supplied useful weapon evidence—and exposed test assumptions that could not be counted as passes.
verificationStatus: Scoped passes; core suite remains incomplete
paragraphs: A local shot should feel immediate even though the server receives it later. The weapon path now measures the client/server time relationship and evaluates a bounded history of player poses. Live characters are not moved backward for the query, and present-day cover still wins. This is a declared prototype policy with limits, not a claim to reconstruct every past moment perfectly.

The delayed-network scenario passed 24 assertions at roughly 216 ms measured round-trip time. It checked that local prediction preceded server acceptance and that state reconciled afterward. A separate moving-target scenario passed ten assertions at roughly 215 ms while the target moved laterally, recording a server-confirmed torso hit and exactly one round spent. Another eight-assertion test observed a bullet in flight before it hit cover about 60 metres away, without damaging a player.

The test work also corrected how brief effects were sampled. A requested short wait can return too late to observe a flash or kick, and a large first-frame delta can consume a new effect before it is shown. Creation-frame preservation and bounded frame sampling replaced that assumption. The flight test likewise needed a corrected fixture before its successful run; its first setup failure remains in the record.

The main core suite remains failed, even though its second attempt passed 78 checks before stopping. It incorrectly required every attempted unreliable request to arrive. The right follow-up must distinguish attempted sends, actual receipts and accepted gameplay costs. Later core checks did not execute, so neither the narrower passes nor the 2,683 deterministic rule and geometry checks can stand in for a completed run.

Recorded hip, aimed and observer holding stills support limited framing review. They do not establish firing rhythm, recoil recovery, muzzle timing, reload quality or accepted audio. All of these network scenarios used two clients and a dedicated server inside one editor process. Broader connection conditions, independent clients, packaged servers and capacity remain future qualification.
highlights: Measured round-trip time kept separate from configured delay
24 delay, 10 moving-target and 8 flight assertions passed separately
2,683 deterministic rule and geometry checks
Transient feedback tested on actual sampled frames
Failed runs preserved with their unexecuted scope
limitations: The core suite is incomplete after two failed attempts
Bounded delay cases do not establish general network fairness or capacity
Moving-target evidence is sampled after a tick, not an exact reconstruction of resolution time
Still images do not establish normal-speed combat presentation
History recovery and broader hit-query conditions remain unqualified

title: Tin Finch: our first original ship
summary: A compact salvage skiff takes shape, with a weathered pressure cabin, exposed engines and an interior built around one pilot.
verificationStatus: Original vehicle asset; native export checks passed
paragraphs: Our first original ship is the Tin Finch TF-01, a single-seat salvage skiff with a patched cabin and its machinery on display. Three rear exhausts, side-mounted tanks, braced landing skids and a narrow boarding step give the small craft its practical character. Its name, geometry, markings and surface artwork were created for this project, with supplied vehicle references informing the utilitarian aesthetic.

The cabin has a modeled pilot seat, gauges, pedals and controls, while a separate hinged hatch opens to reveal the interior. The asset includes four levels of detail, collision proxies and attachment points. Its editable construction remains available alongside the exported hull and hatch, so later integration can work from the actual model rather than a single concept image.

The native Blender previews show the finished asset from the front, rear, open hatch and pilot's seat, alongside a wireframe view. Export and reimport checks preserved mesh counts, dimensions, collision proxies and the recorded UV channels. The portable package also passed structural geometry, material and hatch-animation checks.

This milestone delivers the ship's art and an integration handoff. The renders are Blender previews; flight, boarding interactions and working instruments have not been implemented by this asset package. Bringing Tin Finch into playable form is a separate step.

title: Learning what a small spherical world needs
summary: An isolated Unreal terrain experiment connected six curved terrain faces, collision checks and a first woodland scene, while exposing the gap between correct geometry and a convincing world.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal experiment: bounded collision checks passed
paragraphs: Before the current Godot project, we explored small spherical worlds in an isolated Unreal prototype. The first useful step was a six-section sphere with consistent surface boundaries. An early collision failure turned out to be a triangle-facing problem: the surface could be hit from inside the planet but not reliably from outside. Correcting the triangle order gave us a working control to build on.

That control grew into shaped terrain, ground materials, atmosphere and a woodland scene. The first shaped version contained six terrain faces and 710 decorative woodland actors. Sampled rays and swept shapes checked the actual loaded terrain across faces, seams and corners, with 540 checks passing in the editor and another 540 in a running test session.

The work also made the asset pipeline more repeatable. Existing source archives were inventoried and extracted with integrity checks, while a separate native terrain experiment was preserved after two unsuccessful builds. Keeping the working terrain and the unresolved experiment separate let the visual study continue without treating an unproven engine feature as a finished foundation.

The next visual revision was rejected on 3 October because the geography did not meet the project's quality goal. More detail and vegetation could not solve that by themselves. These results belong to an early Unreal study: the collision samples did not prove physical walking around a planet, streaming, packaged performance or a finished environment, and they are not validation of today's Godot worlds.

Built and sampled six shaped terrain faces
Added an initial woodland and atmosphere study
Preserved failed experiments and visual feedback alongside the passes

The later visual revision was rejected
Collision sampling did not qualify radial walking, streaming or a complete planet

title: A survival loop that remembers what happened
summary: The Unreal prototype connected paid crafting, deployables, death, corpse looting, respawn and reconnect to persistent server-owned state.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal prototype: scoped gameplay and recovery checks passed
paragraphs: The 3 October survival milestone connected actions that had previously been separate experiments. In the historical Unreal prototype, crafting consumed ingredients, sleeping bags and cupboards used server-checked placement, death transferred belongings into loot, and respawn created a new life. The server kept ownership of those changes so an old request could not repeat a purchase or claim the same belongings twice.

A dedicated test map put two clients through crafting, placement, cupboard permissions, corpse looting and bag or beach respawn. All 74 checks in that scenario passed. The test deliberately used supplied resources and shortened bag timing, so it demonstrated the connected rules without claiming a complete gathering loop or normal-world balance.

Disconnecting also became part of the world. A player left behind a vulnerable sleeping body, and reconnecting reclaimed that body's identity and saved state. A later focused check verified the sleeping overlay and an explicit key press to wake. Separate orderly restart comparisons checked that inventory, life, health, bag identities and sampled world entities survived reopening the same save.

There were still real limits. A cold startup exceeded the persistence completion deadline before a warm retry succeeded; forced game-process crashes, broad coastal play, production accounts and population scale were not qualified. Some survival visuals were placeholders. This is a record of the earlier Unreal milestone, not a claim that its code or every test result carries over to the current Godot game.

title: Building a base, then making its damage consistent
summary: Snapped construction, grades, cupboard access, doors and locks became a connected Unreal prototype, followed by shared firearm and explosive damage rules.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal prototype: builds passed; gameplay acceptance remained partial
paragraphs: Base building became a substantial playable slice in the earlier Unreal project. A building plan placed modular pieces, a hammer repaired and upgraded them, and cupboard permissions controlled construction. The prototype covered twenty structural parts and five grades, with doors and code locks treated as separate inventory-backed objects rather than properties hidden inside a wall.

The separation mattered when things changed. An open, unlocked door could be removed under its own rules; locks had their own authorization and removal conditions; destroying a support had to remove dependent pieces consistently. Focused play checks covered cupboard storage and permissions, a stone upgrade, repair feedback, direct explosive damage and save recovery. Later manual play exposed additional problems in half-wall contacts, stairs, ceiling selection and movement while the build wheel was open, which led to another correction pass.

Damage then gained a common calculation and receiver boundary. Firearms and timed explosives could share editable attack and defense definitions while characters, structures and doors retained their own consequences. A two-client check observed bullets damaging twig and wood, leaving stronger structural grades unchanged, and damaging a wooden door independently of its frame. A duplicate fire request did not create a second ammunition cost or hit.

Successful builds and thousands of rule checks did not make the whole slice finished. The damage scenario stopped at an interaction outside its allowed reach, later corrections still needed manual acceptance, and upkeep, decay, area explosions and a broader arsenal were outside this milestone. These were historical Unreal systems; the current Godot ground game has its own implementation and validation history.
highlights: Connected snapped building, repair, upgrades and cupboard permissions
Separated structures, doors and code locks
Checked direct explosive damage and scoped save recovery
Introduced shared, editable firearm and explosive damage definitions
limitations: Historical Unreal prototype, not a current Godot feature checklist
Later building and damage changes retained manual acceptance work
Upkeep, decay and area explosions were not delivered in this slice

title: A private playtest package, and an honest startup limit
summary: The Unreal prototype was packaged for a host and a friend, with separate profiles and reconnect identities; a memory failure kept the full two-computer playtest unverified.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal package built; end-to-end private playtest not verified
paragraphs: The next practical goal was simple: let two people try the historical Unreal prototype without opening the editor. We built a standalone package and reusable launchers so one computer could host a headless game process while both players joined as clients. Persistent player and server profiles lived outside the replaceable package, allowing an update without bundling or replacing anybody's world save.

The private development setup created a local reconnect identity and used a private network for access. It was a playtest arrangement, not a public account service. The headless host loaded the intended world with no local player, opened its network endpoint, and completed an observed orderly stop and restart. It used the packaged game executable; it was not a separately compiled dedicated-server target.

Trying to join exposed two different startup problems. The initial client reached the join stage but spent most of its readiness window loading the world, so the startup logic was adjusted to separate world travel from player admission. A rebuilt and repackaged attempt then exhausted available Windows committed memory while the server and client started together, and both processes exited.

The launchers were updated to wait for actual world-load completion and refuse a local join while the host was still loading or had failed. Those final safeguards received syntax checks, but there was no successful final runtime retry. Packaging was completed; authenticated spawn, reconnect, packaged save recovery and play across two computers remained open. This entry records an Unreal prototype boundary, not the hosting status of today's Godot project.
highlights: Built a standalone private playtest package
Separated persistent server and player profiles from game updates
Observed headless world load and orderly restart
Improved startup checks after loading and memory failures

The final server-and-client attempt failed under memory pressure
End-to-end admission and external two-computer play remained unverified

title: Giving the prototype its own doors, tools and ship art
summary: Original supplied kits replaced survival placeholders and expanded the art library, while resource harvesting and Tin Finch flight stayed explicitly separate from importing their models.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal integration: build and asset checks passed; gameplay not tested
paragraphs: The 4–5 October art pass gave several working Unreal prototype systems more suitable visuals. The sleeping bag and tool cupboard received supplied project art. Six single and double door variants gained authored frames and hinged leaves, while the existing gameplay still owned placement, opening, health, condition, permissions and persistence.

Keeping art separate from rules made this a controlled replacement. Item identities, recipe costs and save formats stayed intact. Door frames joined the placement-clearance checks, and the final source correction ensured their collision could be queried correctly. A successful native build and saved asset readback confirmed the bindings; they did not substitute for testing the doors during play.

The handoff also staged four resource families with intact, fractured and remnant forms, alongside workbench, tool and other prop art. Tin Finch's hull and hatch were imported with their materials, levels of detail and collision. Its attachment markers did not import correctly, so an attempted assembly was rolled back and the unresolved attachment work remained documented.

This milestone was about admitting and connecting art in the historical Unreal prototype. It did not enable resource harvesting, new vehicle recipes or a flyable ship, and no gameplay scenarios were run for this integration. Those distinctions matter in the archive: a model visible in an editor is not yet a working game system, and later Godot work needs its own integration and acceptance.

title: When world population forced a foundation rethink
summary: A failed vegetation-heavy Unreal map led to World Partition, runtime vegetation generation and a documented architecture rebuild, with measured progress and clear unfinished work.
verificationStatus: Historical Unreal milestone: world conversion and scoped editor play verified
paragraphs: The earlier Unreal project reached a practical limit when a vegetation pass saved roughly 9.9 million instances into a single map. Playing that version exhausted the development machine's memory. We preserved the failed checkpoint and restored the playable map before changing how the world was organized. The problem was recorded as a failed approach, not hidden behind a larger content count.

The replacement converted a copy of the world to World Partition with three-dimensional cells and grouped distant geometry. Vegetation moved to runtime generation in separate tree, concealment and ground-cover roles. The converted map became the default, and actual editor play showed terrain, vegetation and a previously saved player base together.

The recorded editor private-memory use dropped from roughly 25 GB to roughly 6 GB while idle. A dedicated-server-and-client editor session still used about 20 GB with vegetation, so this was progress with a substantial remaining cost. These were development-machine observations, not a packaged-game benchmark, player-capacity result or promise that arbitrary world sizes would work.

An accompanying audit set out a broader Unreal rebuild around engine-supported gameplay components and editable data. Only the world milestone was completed; the new data layer had begun and compiled but was not yet in use. Inventory, combat, persistence and interface migration still lay ahead. That branch is part of the project's history before the current Godot direction, whose architecture and world limits are documented separately.

Converted a world copy to three-dimensional World Partition
Generated vegetation at runtime by habitat role
Measured lower idle editor memory and documented the unfinished rebuild

title: The first foundations of Hollow Universe
summary: The first galaxy and system maps established a deterministic world foundation and an interface built around readable exploration.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: initial generator and maps implemented
paragraphs: This retrospective begins with the first recorded Hollow Universe build on 10 October. A galaxy generator, galaxy map and star-system map made it possible to move from a broad view of space into individual systems. This was the beginning of a new foundation in C# and Godot, with generation and simulation kept separate from the engine that presents them.

Deterministic generation was central to that foundation. A system's address and seed needed to describe the same place every time, independently of which part of the map happened to be open. Keeping those rules outside the renderer made it possible to examine and test the generated universe without starting the full game.

The interface received attention immediately. Real-pixel scaling, clearer typography, values beside their labels and collision-aware map labels made information easier to read at different resolutions. The aim was to let the player understand the selected place without losing it beneath panels or overlapping names.

The original astronomical scale was an early exploration of the idea, not the current playable-world specification. Hollow Universe has since adopted a maximum of 1,000 stars and much smaller planets. The generation and map work described here remains a foundation; its original scale should not be mistaken for a promise about the game being built today.

C# generation and simulation separated from Godot presentation
Deterministic addresses and seeds
Readable map typography and labels across resolutions

title: Giving star systems their own identity
summary: Stellar ages, multiple-star orbits and physical planet descriptions gave the generator a richer vocabulary for building distinct places.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: generator improvements implemented and tested
paragraphs: Looking back at 12 October, the generator moved beyond arranging stars and planets into attractive diagrams. Stars gained ages and evolutionary outcomes, including evolved stars and remnants. Multiple-star systems gained an orbit structure that could describe planets circling a companion or a pair of stars, rather than forcing every system into a single-star template.

Planets and moons received richer physical descriptions. Composition, atmosphere, climate, geology and biosphere state became the basis for their classifications and hazards. The purpose was to make a world's identity emerge from related properties, so that its description could eventually inform what a player finds there.

An authored layer added familiar stars, real planetary systems and named regions alongside procedural generation. The work also strengthened reproducibility checks and made changes to generated output explicit. Optional reference data should enrich the catalogue without unpredictably changing unrelated generated places.

Three interactive map concepts explored different approaches to search, zoom and reach. They were experiments in usability, not a final map design or proof of navigable space. The current project reuses the system-generation work within a smaller galaxy and compact planets; direct travel and the final space presentation remain separate implementation work.

Orbits around individual stars and multiple-star systems
Planetary composition, atmosphere and climate descriptions
Authored real systems alongside deterministic generation
Three interactive map-interface concepts

title: A survival game takes shape
summary: Networking, gathering, crafting, building and combat came together on a rendered planetary surface, with persistent characters and hosted multiplayer checks.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: integrated prototype with scoped multiplayer checks
paragraphs: The ground work on 12 October turned the project into a connected survival prototype. A dedicated .NET server decided the results of player actions, while the client predicted movement and displayed other players smoothly. Characters could survive a server restart, and early multiplayer checks exercised the connection before the world and gameplay layers grew around it.

Gathering, crafting, containers, survival stats, melee and bows were connected to a first-person HUD and inventory. Death, corpses and sleeping characters gave possessions a place in the world beyond a single session. Terrain, ocean, sky, vegetation and shader grass then replaced the initial presentation placeholders, bringing those rules into an actual landscape.

Building added structural pieces, grades, doors, locks, stability, upkeep and collapse. Networked placement spent real inventory resources and survived restarts. Firearms brought server-resolved bullet flight, ammunition, attachments, armour and a wounded state. Raiding connected explosives, blast shielding and structural destruction, including attacks on bases whose owners were offline.

Models, sound and effects were integrated alongside the rules so that building, gathering and combat could be seen and heard in hosted play. Development exercises included separate 100-bot survival, building, combat and raid scenarios, plus captures with two players and 50 bots. These are bounded historical checks on the recorded setup, not a guarantee of supported player capacity or current performance.

Connected gathering, crafting, inventory and survival
Networked building, upkeep and structural collapse
Firearms, armour, wounded players and explosives

title: From the first base to the Tin Finch
summary: The starter spacecraft entered the connected game alongside recycling, research, technology trees, teams and a growing wildlife loop.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: connected gameplay and local-flight checks
paragraphs: By the morning of 13 October, the Tin Finch had moved from a vehicle asset and development sandbox into the connected ground game. Players could craft it at a Vehicle Workbench, board through its hatch and fly from the cockpit or a chase camera. Fuel, boost, landing and crash consequences gave the small craft a practical role beyond simply moving the camera above the ground.

The same integration brought salvage, components, loot containers, recycling, workbench technology trees and the Research Bench into the playable loop. Blueprints could be learned, materials could be recovered from unwanted loot, and technology provided goals beyond collecting another stack of resources. Teams, teammate markers and a shared map helped players coordinate those activities.

Wildlife added another source of risk and useful materials. Deer, boars, wolves and bears had movement and attack behavior, while carcasses supplied meat and other crafting resources. A recorded development exercise combined 100 survival bots with 200 animals to investigate the cost of those systems together. It was a specific stress scenario, not a statement about the population of every part of the world.

The F1 console also became a useful playtesting tool, with server-checked commands, item browsing and live connection information. The recorded integration included hosted screenshots of crafting, research, teams, boarding and flight. The Tin Finch milestone established local planetary flight; continuous travel to another planet or star system was still outside its scope.

title: Making every action read clearly
summary: Playtest feedback led to clearer gathering, consistent interaction and placement, better lootbags, and a loading process that waits for the world.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: focused rules and rendered interaction checks
paragraphs: The 13 October playtests exposed a gap between rules that worked and actions that communicated clearly. Tree and ore hits could be difficult to read, some placement actions lacked a preview, and important interactions were hidden behind inconsistent controls. This pass focused on making the same actions understandable in the player's hands.

Trees gained a moving painted weak spot, visible reactions and better-timed felling feedback. Ore nodes gained surface-aligned hotspots and staged break effects. Hit feedback was placed at the actual contact point and old hits stopped replaying when an area came into view. Dropped items were gathered into small lootbags, replacing cases where an inventory item appeared on the ground as its full-size world model.

Interaction, placement, held-item behavior and radial menus moved onto shared systems. The placement preview and the server now used the same rules, with a reason shown when an object could not fit. Doors, locks, deployables and the Tin Finch gained consistent placement and interaction paths. Free look, ammunition selection, item information and retrieving arrows from the surfaces they struck also became part of the connected experience.

A staged loading screen waited for the world and renderer to be ready before handing control to the player. Building art received a measured repair pass for gaps, overlapping faces and detail-level transitions, while destruction effects used fragments of the project's actual models. Hosted captures and focused checks supported these changes, but some startup stalls, debris collision limits and character-presentation issues remained for later work.

Lootbags that combine nearby dropped items
Shared placement rules, previews and refusal reasons
Consistent interaction and radial menus
Loading stages, repaired building joints and model-based debris

title: Places to discover, systems to build on
summary: A substantial monument art archive and a clearer shared architecture gave the growing game more room to develop, with better tools for inspecting it.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: built art and architecture checks; monument gameplay unfinished
paragraphs: This retrospective covers the monument work of 13 October and the systems work that followed on 14 October. The monument archive reached 55 built types represented by 57 model variants, supported by 64 shared modular parts. Mining camps, research outposts, launch facilities, wrecks and larger remnants established a visual library for the remains of an earlier civilization.

The distinction between art and gameplay matters here. Models, definitions and previews existed and could be inspected in a dedicated viewer. Their full placement rules, encounters, rewards and site interactions were still separate work. The archive is a resource for the current compact-world design, which must choose and adapt sites to fit its planets rather than inherit every earlier scale assumption.

As the survival game grew, its internal structure was reorganized around registered systems with clearer responsibilities. Simulation rules, network handlers, data readers and client and server modules were separated from the hosts that coordinate them. The aim was practical: adding another feature should extend the shared systems instead of creating a new special case across the whole game.

The F2 developer panel made that structure visible during play. title: A whole world, and a ship you can walk around
summary: Spherical ground, a globe-to-chart map and the crewed Iron Wake expanded the foundation, while integrated playtesting remained essential.
verificationStatus: Retrospective: implemented systems with remaining integrated playtests
paragraphs: The 15 October world milestone extended the ground game to a complete sphere. Terrain, sea, the horizon and vegetation followed the planet's shape, while falling objects and movement used the local direction of gravity. One world map could transition between a globe and a flat chart, sharing location references with navigation and respawn views.

The walking-ground work added sixteen surface layers derived from the project's owned scans, along with lakes and streams rendered as water. Captures made it possible to inspect forests, plains, mountains and coasts at ground level. The Iron Wake explored a different scale of play: a large crewed spacecraft whose decks can be walked and furnished. Its implementation brought ship-relative movement, multiple seats, doors, crewed batteries, building aboard and incendiary fire. Interior lights, sound and effects gave those systems a presentation layer, while model repairs closed hull openings and improved the visible loading machinery.

title: Hollow Universe: our name and the direction ahead
summary: We are Hollow Universe. The current game starts on Earth with a rock and a torch, building toward a compact, persistent survival sandbox among the stars.
verificationStatus: Current design confirmed; compact Earth foundation verified
paragraphs: We are now Hollow Universe. The name belongs to the project we are building today: a sandbox survival game set after humanity's near-extinction, where advanced technology coexists with equipment and structures that people make themselves. This update brings the site's identity into line with that direction and looks back at the concrete foundation established on 15 October.

The journey begins on Earth with one rock and one torch. Gathering, looting and crafting lead into a first base, stronger equipment, resource control and eventually spacecraft. Full-loot PvP and offline raiding remain part of the design, alongside the requirement that exploration and production give a lone player worthwhile things to do. The familiar ground interface is being preserved while the wider game develops around it.

The scale is now explicit: at most 1,000 stars, and no planet larger than approximately 23.04 square kilometres across its entire surface. The current Earth implementation has a radius of 1,200 metres and about 18.10 square kilometres of surface. The default finite galaxy contains 1,000 stars across 610 systems. Direct flight between planets and systems, without a separate supercruise mode, is the intended travel experience; completing that connected journey remains work ahead.

Separate Vehicle and Engineering Workbenches are part of the new foundation. The Tin Finch requires its vehicle technology and station, while the Engineering Workbench exists without an invented technology catalogue. Local flight now crosses the old orbital marker and returns under ordinary controls, within the current planet's flight volume. The compact Earth milestone passed all 298 recorded gameplay and supporting checks, with clean builds, inspected menu and world captures, and a saved character successfully rejoining after restart.

That successful baseline is a milestone, not the whole design delivered. Later repairs have their own status in the next journal entry. Travel between worlds, modular upgrades, electricity, oxygen equipment and other systems still need connected implementation and validation. Surveying, wreck recovery, factory networks and repeatable monument activities are proposals being considered for long-term play, rather than features we are announcing as already available.
highlights: Hollow Universe is the current project identity
Earth start with exactly one rock and one torch
Maximum 1,000 stars and 23.04 km² per planet's entire surface
Vehicle progression and continuous local ascent and return
298/298 checks passed at the compact Earth baseline
limitations: Continuous travel between planets and star systems is not yet complete
The 298/298 result predates the subsequent repair work
Long-term activity proposals remain distinct from implemented features
No release date or production player-capacity claim

title: The repair pass: controls, survival and the Salvaged Axe
summary: The latest pass improves ship handling, inventory input and breathing, adds the Salvaged Axe, and keeps unresolved checks visible.
verificationStatus: Scoped repairs verified; full checkpoint 330/334, work continues
paragraphs: This entry records the repair work following the compact Earth baseline on 15 October. The focus is on how the existing game behaves in the player's hands. Ships now retain movement commands when the helm is empty and have explicit engine controls. Steering and throttle were revised, and every seat gained a player-centred orbit-camera path. Focused flight and save checks passed, while the combined mouse gestures and seated presentation still needed live review.

Inventory improvements include rotating the character preview, more reliable hover-looting and native windowed, borderless and exclusive display settings. Actual interface-input checks covered the new gestures, and native display-mode checks confirmed the requested modes. Weapon presentation also received fixes to existing hand and bow paths, but initial captures exposed further problems; a complete held-item animation and visual-authoring pass remains active work.

Survival now has a shared breathing rule that checks the player's eye against the local water surface, including lakes and streams. Reserve, recovery, drowning and saved breathing state were exercised, and the HUD can show oxygen. Animals were also prevented from biting through blocking structures or attacking players protected by supported floors and foundations. The Salvaged Axe joined the item catalogue as a stronger woodcutting tool with its own imported model, inventory icons and editable held-item profile. Focused checks covered finding and learning the blueprint, workbench requirements, crafting and harvesting. First-person, third-person and swing captures were inspected. The latest recorded full run at this checkpoint passed 330 of 334 checks, including the new axe coverage. Four failures remained in the shared repair work, so the earlier 298/298 baseline cannot be used to call this later state clean. Follow-up fixes and visual review are continuing. title: A workshop for hands, grips and held-item motion
summary: A standalone editor now brings item placement, hand posing and action keyframes into the same first- and third-person renderers used by the game.
verificationStatus: Working editor preview; animation polish and wider validation remain in progress
paragraphs: Getting a held item right means more than moving a model into the camera. The grip, fingers, shoulders and motion all have to agree, and the result must work both in the player’s hands and on the character other people see. The new held-item workshop puts those controls beside a live preview, with a searchable item library and first-person, arms-orbit and third-person views.

The screenshot shows the bow’s draw action at 60% of its authored timeline. Placement, Hands and Motion tabs separate the rest grip from the action. The editor exposes position and rotation, hand offsets, finger poses, keyframe interpolation and the event marker. Scrubbing lets us inspect a particular moment; playback shows how the anticipation, event and recovery connect.

The preview uses the game’s existing first-person and character renderers. Gameplay timing can align an authored event with the simulation’s tick-based action duration. The visible target and contact adjustment are authoring aids: an edited pose does not award a hit, change reach, consume ammunition or alter the server’s rules.

Profiles are saved as validated project JSON, with undo, redo, reload and protection against overwriting external changes. This is an active tool and presentation pass, not a claim that every grip and animation is finished. The workshop also exposes arm-reach correction so a pose that needs adjustment is visible during authoring. The images here show the actual editor, including the owner’s bow-motion capture and a fresh third-person capture from the current build.

title: Admin tools, shadow budgets and a way out of the game
summary: Free building and crafting for testers, a third-person admin camera, loading and shadow fixes, and a DISCONNECT button that lets go cleanly.
verificationStatus: Checked in focused builds and native runs; wider combat and performance work continues
paragraphs: The sixteenth of October was repair-wave work: the unglamorous changes that make a survival game faster to test. The F1 console’s TOOLS tab gained a BUILDING section. BGRADE places structural pieces at a chosen tier (Twig, Wood, Stone, Metal or Armoured) at full health, and FREE BUILD covers construction, upgrades, hammer repairs, keys and repeated placement without resource costs. A matching free-crafting switch shows every recipe and skips ingredients, blueprints and workbench requirements while keeping ordinary crafting times.

These are admin switches, not shortcuts around the rules. Reach, collision, support, claim authorisation and ownership limits are still enforced, explosive charges are still consumed, and the flags live only in the session: they reset on reconnect or when admin rights are revoked, and they are never written into a save. The admin camera is the other tester’s tool. A THIRD PERSON mode orbits the player with the right mouse button, zooms from 1.5 to 20 metres and draws the full character, with clothing, held item and stance, using the same renderer other players see.

The Esc menu now has DISCONNECT. It returns to PLAY / CONNECT with the address form open, without closing the game; a locally hosted server saves and stops, and a remote one keeps running. A native test drove real keyboard and mouse events through hosting, disconnecting, connecting to a second server, disconnecting again and re-hosting on the first port, and checked that the old session’s views, audio and inventory preview were torn down cleanly.

Two loading and performance changes landed too. The last loading stage, which waits for steady frames, could wait forever below 30 FPS once everything was ready; it now has a five-second deadline. A new SHADOWS settings tab exposes sun cascades (1, 2 or 4), shadow quality and distance, and a budget of 0 to 8 local shadow lights shared by ship lamps, weapon beams and torches. In one isolated test, two cascades cut draw calls from 1,561 to 1,161 and the mean frame from 16.40 to 15.73 ms. That is one scene on one graphics card, not a general promise.

title: Wires, wind power, a centred crosshair and Drop All
summary: A first electricity foundation powers a defence line from a windmill, the HUD marker becomes a setting, and one button empties a backpack.
verificationStatus: Foundation implemented and focused-tested; static ground wiring only
paragraphs: Electricity now has a foundation instead of ad-hoc power flags. Devices declare physical ports in data, amber for outputs and cyan for inputs, and a new Wire Tool runs a cable from an output through optional surface anchors to an input. The server enforces a 20-metre limit between endpoint ports, rejects cycles and occupied ports, checks rights at both ends and refuses cables whose route is obstructed. Circuits nobody is editing do no work each tick, and a test touching one circuit among 1,000 unrelated ones confirmed that rebuilding stays local.

Three production items are wired so far: the windmill, the auto turret and the SAM site. In the review scene, wind power runs through the turret and on to the SAM, and a consumer that is off or under-supplied passes whatever power remains onward. Alongside it, shared device authorisation records who may use a device. It stores grants and exclusions, lets a device follow its tool cupboard or be set to manual only, and gives a newly placed, unclaimed device its placer’s protection. The SAM uses the pilot’s identity, so a passenger in the seat does not make it friendly.

The crosshair is now a setting. The owner asked for one centred marker instead of a separate dot and firearm ticks, with a dot as the default. The CROSSHAIR tab offers Off, Dot, Cross, Cross + Dot, Ring and Ring + Dot, six colours, and size, dot size, thickness, gap, opacity and outline, with a live preview drawn by the same code as the in-game marker. Optional dynamic spread widens crosses and rings while firing from the hip. A native check of 53 conditions measured the rendered pixels at two resolutions and two interface scales and found the marker exactly at the centre (0 px error).

A small inventory change completes the batch. DROP ALL sits beside INVENTORY and drops the 24 backpack slots only, leaving the belt, worn equipment and any open loot alone. The server treats it as one all-or-nothing request, so a stale inventory rejects the whole action and the client’s prediction rolls back instead of leaving half a stack on the ground.
