title: A meadow worth walking through
summary: Thirty-four ground textures, grass rebuilt as clumps of several species, and recorded footsteps that depend on surface and footwear.
verificationStatus: Measured in the game on one machine; owner look review still pending
paragraphs: The owner’s captures of the meadow showed three problems: a quilt of half-metre squares of grass and bare mud, mud under every tuft, and a flat, blurry beach. The squares came from the grass itself, which gave each cell either a whole tuft or nothing. Now every cell where grass grows has a tuft, and its cards come and go one by one as density changes. The ground under the grass was the second cause: the scan used beneath it was trampled mud. The ground now carries 34 4K textures, the original sixteen plus alternatives chosen per pixel, so lush grass grows over a green grass-ground scan and the beach is pebbly sand.

On 20 October the grass itself was rebuilt. It is now drawn as clumps modelled in Blender from text: field grass, tall grass in seed, dry grass, flower clumps, heather or leafy herbs, and litter, with a hand-painted atlas, real normals and cheap distant levels. One coverage rule decides what grows where from the terrain’s own climate (meadow, forest edge, forest floor, dry, tundra). Flowers are back at about six per cent of a meadow’s clumps, and blade colour follows the ground’s tint at its root. Clumps are built in 16-cell tiles on worker threads and uploaded a few per frame.

The result also costs less. In the same test clearing on one graphics card, the High preset’s GPU frame fell from about 21.3 ms to 15.7–16.7 ms, and on the owner’s own lower-detail profile from 9.3 to 4.7 ms; the primitives drawn fell from 12.5 million to 8.0 million. Removing the new grass makes the frame slower, because the clumps hide expensive terrain pixels. The extra textures are not free: about 2.0 GB of files and 1.7 GB of video memory, so the Low preset skips the alternatives.

Footsteps got the same treatment. On 18 October the old grass and dirt steps were replaced by recorded banks, then extended to eight surfaces: grass, dirt, sand, rock, snow, wood, metal and shallow water. A library of 193 recorded source clips produces 579 sound files in three footwear profiles, barefoot, shoes and boots, and the work boots in the game today select the boots profile. The footwear sound is a treatment applied to one recorded library, not separate recordings of each shoe; a future shoe item only needs to name a profile.

title: Doors that behave the same from both sides
summary: Symmetric doors, hinge and swing chosen separately, doors that never refuse to move, and airlocks that fall out of the rules.
verificationStatus: Built, unit-tested and photographed in the hosted game; owner decisions on two defaults are pending
paragraphs: On 20 October the owner reported that our doors behaved nothing like Rust’s, and a read-only audit confirmed each point. One leaf had a detailed face and a flat one, hinge side and swing direction were tied together by a single 180-degree flip, a door refused to move if someone stood in the way, and collision jumped to the end pose while the animation was still travelling. The owner’s rules were written down as DOORS.md: both faces alike, doors that ignore everything and always move, collision that follows the real motion, hinge and swing chosen separately so airlocks can be built, and locks on both faces.

Four work packages followed within a day. Every leaf is now symmetric and sits inside its frame; the earlier kit had doors standing proud of them. A door has a layout: hinge on the left or right, swinging in or out, so a single door has four layouts, a double door two and the garage door one, and R steps through them when placing. A door is a motion record, a start tick and a direction, and its progress at any tick is arithmetic: a leaf swings in 30 ticks, a garage curtain rolls in 90. The server poses every body each tick, a closing leaf pushes anyone in its way out through the doorway rather than refusing, and the client predicts the same motion.

Airlocks fall out of those rules. Tests flood-fill the floor with the character’s capsule to prove that two doors whose open leaves end up in a small room really do block the walkway between them, including the owner’s own arrangement with both doors swinging in. The pictures are from the hosted game: a triangular airlock seen from above with its leaf swung in, a double door shut from outside, and a square room with a double door and a single door.

Under load, a build test with 30 bots made 238 door toggles with 36,030 reconciliations and no corrections, at 1.47 ms per server tick. Door items were redrawn from the corrected kit and lightened to about 5,000–6,000 triangles at the highest level of detail. A review also found that an open garage door still held a box 2.4 m into the storey above it; its body is now only the part still hanging below the header.

title: One module system for a car, a bike, a helicopter and a boat
summary: Four vehicle efforts agreed on one shared foundation: the TOGG, the Zamazingo, the KA-FA 1500 and a small motorboat.
verificationStatus: Core and first vehicles built and tested; art and feel are first passes the owner is still judging
paragraphs: Four vehicle efforts ran side by side on 20 October and agreed to share one foundation. The core is a module system: a vehicle kind declares sockets, modules (cabins, engines, decks, storage) declare what they fit, and a composer builds the result and applies rules between parts. Each module has its own hold and its own health; shots and blasts find module bodies, the hammer repairs them through the same path as buildings, and the whole build is saved and sent with the vehicle. The same system is meant to serve ground vehicles, a rotorcraft and, later, spacecraft.

On top of it sit the TOGG, the modular car, and the Zamazingo, the motorbike (both names are the owner’s), crafted at the Vehicle Workbench and learned in its tech tree. The TOGG’s motor is a sprung-wheel ground motor with tyre grip, drive, brakes and steering; the first version stood, reached 19.5 m/s, climbed a 20° slope but not a 42° one, and gave identical results run twice. The owner’s first ride on the bike was blunt: not rideable. The fault was contact: wheel boxes with flat faces stopped it dead on a 15 cm step. Every wheel is now a round cylinder swept along its travel, so a tyre climbs a kerb the way a real one does. The measured 0–50 km/h time fell from 2.2 to 1.6 s, and the bike now clears kerbs of more than 25 cm from a crawl.

The KA-FA 1500, our minicopter, hovers with no input, moves by tilting, levels itself and weathercocks its tail; its lift follows the rotor’s spool squared and the thinning air, which gives it a ceiling. Its rotors turn from the spool, and its sound is built in code from the spool and collective. An automated tour flew it out and back to its pad in 96 seconds and touched down at 0.1 m/s, unhurt. The motorboat floats on six buoyancy columns, is driven by an outboard that pushes only while under water, is placed on water rather than land, and is crafted in 60 seconds at a level 1 workbench.

People matter too. Riders weigh on a vehicle’s springs at 85 kg each, and landings rock it; running people over is specified; engines can be switched on by hand; and the vehicle workbench’s bay is now marked on the ground with hazard-stripe paint and corner posts, after the owner could not see where it was.
highlights: One module core shared by car, bike, minicopter and boat
TOGG and Zamazingo crafted at the Vehicle Workbench
Round tyres that climb kerbs; bike 0–50 km/h in 1.6 s
KA-FA 1500 rotor drive with a spool, a ceiling and a flown tour
Motorboat with buoyancy columns and an underwater-only outboard
limitations: The first TOGG and Zamazingo were drawn as blocks; the models in these pictures arrived later and are still being polished

title: A bay you drive into, and a TOGG that sounds like a truck
summary: Tyres, a lift kit and engines can be changed at the vehicle workbench, and the TOGG gains an overboost, black smoke and a recorded diesel.
verificationStatus: Rules tested over the network and in a hosted tour; frame times and sound balance are not yet measured
paragraphs: The owner asked how to change a car’s engine or tyres, and until 21 October the answer was that you could not: the build was fixed when the car was crafted. Tyres and suspension are now modules too. A TOGG takes stock tyres, 1.7 m monster tyres or a lift kit that raises the body 0.75 m, with rules between them: monster tyres need the kit, and stock tyres exclude it. The Monster TOGG is no longer a separate vehicle but a TOGG with monster parts: 1,920 kg, 450 kW and a 122 km/h top speed on 1.7 m tyres.

The vehicle workbench’s painted bay is the lift. A stopped, empty vehicle standing in the bay can have its build changed: hold E, or open VEHICLE IN BAY from the tech tree, and the vehicle’s sockets appear as slots beside the inventory. Drag a module in to fit it and out to take it off. The server checks everything, from the player’s distance to whether everyone is out of the vehicle, and refuses in plain words, such as ‘Take off the monster tyres first’. Two owner reports shaped the rest. The screen kept asking for a vehicle to be driven into a bay the TOGG was standing in, because the client painted the bay in a different frame from the one the rules measured; the rules now read the bay where it is painted. And a vehicle driven near the bay should be drawn into it: below 4 m/s and within 1.5 m, it glides to the bay’s middle over half a second.
INSPECT VEHICLE, a hold-E verb on any module-built vehicle, opens the same screen read-only from anywhere, with every module’s condition as a bar and a percentage and the chassis health beside it.

The TOGG itself was pushed toward a heavy truck. Left Shift is an overboost: 40 per cent more power at double the fuel, with no time limit, a turbo that spools sooner, a column of black exhaust with billows thrown in the engine’s rhythm, an engine that rocks on its mounts and shakes the chassis, and air brakes that hiss as it comes to rest. Its diesel now plays from recorded truck loops between 600 and 2,400 rpm, with turbo flutter, gear clunks and a Jake brake, instead of a synthesised engine.
highlights: Stock tyres, monster tyres, a 0.75 m lift kit and engines as swappable modules
The Monster TOGG is a TOGG with monster parts
Bay lift with server-checked rules and plain refusals; vehicles glide into the bay
INSPECT VEHICLE shows module and chassis condition from anywhere
Overboost, black smoke, a rocking engine and recorded diesel loops
limitations: A vehicle left in a bay without tyres falls after a server restart
Locking and naming at the bench, engine parts with quality tiers, and the bike’s modules are not built yet
A report that a vehicle cannot be used once its engine is removed has not been reproduced in tests
Frame times with the new smoke and sound are unmeasured: the hosted runs shared the PC with other tests
The truck sound is a first pass; mixing and levels are still being tuned
The pictures are hosted captures; the vehicle screen with the mannequin is the interface viewer on sample data

title: Rebuilding Earth’s terrain, and what we threw away
summary: The first cliff dressing was rejected. Earth is now baked and eroded once, and steep rock comes from a placed kit.
verificationStatus: Fast iterations for the owner to judge by eye; no terrain look is approved and the terrain tests are stale
paragraphs: Terrain was the hardest argument of the week. The first dressing of Earth’s cliffs, scanned rock skins laid along whole faces, went through four generations on 19 October. The owner’s playtest on 20 October found six problems: collision tiles at cliffs reaching 436,000 triangles, 97 per cent of them copied cliff shells; cliffs that read as scattered assets; bare beaches; ground textures repeating in visible squares; white pans of very shallow sea filled with a 3.1 m foam texture; and a shoreline that never moved. The owner rejected the cliffs.

The replacement plan was approved the same day: the ground keeps to runnable slopes, each planet’s large shape is baked once with erosion and drainage, and steep rock becomes placed models from a cliff kit. Earth is now baked on a 7.4 m grid of 393,216 cells and worn by 100 steps: lakes fill to their spill, streams cut by stream power, steep slopes slide and soil creeps. The bake takes about 13.5 seconds, is cached and loads in 0.1 s. It produces 12 lakes (46.8 ha), and its highest ground is 220 m, lower than the designed peaks, because erosion wears them down.

The cliff kit is 21 rock pieces cut from the owner’s scans. A placement pass grows chains of pieces along slopes steeper than 32°, picks a family by place (Nordic near the sea, desert on tablelands, tundra elsewhere), faces each piece downhill and drops any that would stand in water or on a monument. On Earth that was 7,527 pieces in 695 of 6,144 cells, placed in 0.8 s, and the ground is stamped to meet each wall. Collision was cut too: a ground tile keeps only the cliff triangles lying over it, 75,000–100,000 at the six busiest sites instead of 282,000–436,000.

This is deliberately fast, hand-checked iteration. By the owner’s rule, no tests, captures or polish are produced until a look is approved, so several terrain tests currently fail in the working tree, among them the terrain’s golden hash and the cliff placement and formation tests. The cliff picture here is the rejected generation, shown as a record of what we moved away from. Rivers on the baked terrain come next.
highlights: Earth baked once on a 7.4 m grid with 100 erosion steps; cached and loaded in 0.1 s
A 21-piece cliff kit cut from the owner’s scans, placed in 0.8 s
Cliff collision per tile cut from 282,000–436,000 triangles to 75,000–100,000
The rejected cliff generation retired rather than patched
limitations: No terrain look is approved yet; every iteration is for the owner to judge by hand
Tests for Earth’s cliffs, formations and save revision have not been updated: ten fail in the current tree
The cliffs pictured are the rejected 19 October generation
